 US Lawmakers Push to Block Chinese Aircraft Certification and Curb Aerospace Investments
 BY KALUM SHASHI ISHARA 
 Published 4 hours ago 
 0 COMMENTS 
 registration page
 - Dismiss (x) hides the bar for the current page view only
============================================================ -->
 A bipartisan congressional commission is urging the United States government to deny certification to Chinese-made commercial aircraft and impose new restrictions on American investment in China's aerospace industry, according to recommendations reviewed ahead of their official release.
 The House Select Committee on China, which advises Congress on the national security implications of the economic relationship between the two nations, has outlined a series of measures aimed at slowing Beijing's rise as a competitor to American aerospace giants. The proposals come as China pushes to establish its state-owned Commercial Aircraft Corporation of China, known as COMAC, as a credible rival to Boeing and Airbus.
 Certification Concerns
 The committee is recommending that the Federal Aviation Administration refrain from certifying any Chinese-manufactured commercial aircraft for operation in the United States. Certification by the FAA is widely considered a gold standard in global aviation and would open doors for Chinese planemakers to sell their jets in markets around the world.
 COMAC's C919 narrowbody jet, designed to compete directly with the Boeing 737 MAX and the Airbus A320neo family, has been a central focus of concern. The aircraft entered commercial service in China in 2023 and relies heavily on Western components, including engines produced by a joint venture between General Electric and France's Safran.
 Lawmakers behind the recommendations argue that granting FAA approval would effectively validate a program that benefits from significant Chinese state support and alleged technology transfers from foreign firms doing business in China.
 Photo: AeroXplorer/ Daniel Mena  
 Investment Restrictions
 Beyond certification, the committee is calling on the Treasury Department to restrict outbound American investment into China's aerospace sector. The recommendations would broaden existing rules that already limit U.S. capital flows into Chinese semiconductor, quantum computing, and artificial intelligence industries.
 The committee's position reflects a growing bipartisan consensus in Washington that American capital and expertise should not help build up industries that may eventually challenge U.S. economic and national security interests. Aerospace, with its dual civilian and military applications, has long been considered a strategic sector.
 The panel is also expected to recommend that the Commerce Department tighten export controls on components and technology sold to Chinese aerospace firms. Such restrictions could affect American suppliers that currently sell parts, avionics, and software to COMAC and other Chinese manufacturers.

 Broader Context
 The recommendations arrive at a sensitive moment in U.S.-China relations. Boeing has long viewed China as one of its most important growth markets, with Chinese carriers historically accounting for a significant share of global aircraft deliveries. Any escalation in aerospace tensions could complicate the American planemaker's efforts to rebuild its business in the country after years of reduced orders tied to trade disputes and the grounding of the 737 MAX.
 At the same time, COMAC has struggled to secure orders outside China and a small number of allied markets. Without FAA or European Union Aviation Safety Agency certification, its aircraft cannot operate in most of the world's largest aviation markets. The committee's recommendation would reinforce a de facto barrier that has already limited the C919's international reach.
 Industry analysts have noted that COMAC's production capacity remains modest compared with Boeing and Airbus, which together deliver more than a thousand commercial aircraft annually. However, Chinese authorities have made clear that building a domestic aerospace champion is a long-term strategic priority, backed by sustained government funding and procurement commitments from state-owned airlines.
 Political Momentum
 The House Select Committee on China does not have the authority to enact policy, but its annual reports have frequently shaped legislation and executive branch decisions. Past recommendations have influenced measures ranging from investment screening to export controls and sanctions targeting Chinese entities.
 Members of Congress from both parties have signaled openness to new restrictions on economic ties with China's defense and dual-use industries. Earlier legislative efforts have targeted Chinese technology firms, biotechnology companies, and shipbuilders, and aerospace may be the next sector to face scrutiny.
 The Biden administration previously issued executive orders limiting American investment in certain Chinese technology sectors, and the current administration has continued to expand the use of economic tools to counter what officials describe as unfair Chinese industrial practices.
 Photo: AeroXplorer/ Thomas Tse  
 Industry Response
 American aerospace companies have generally avoided public comment on the committee's recommendations, mindful of their commercial interests in China. Boeing has repeatedly emphasized the importance of the Chinese market to its long-term outlook, while suppliers that have invested in joint ventures with Chinese partners face potentially difficult decisions if new restrictions take effect.
 Chinese officials have historically rejected U.S. concerns about state support for COMAC and other strategic industries, framing American restrictions as attempts to suppress legitimate competition. Beijing has signaled it will continue to invest in domestic aerospace capabilities regardless of the regulatory stance adopted in Washington.
 What Comes Next
 Whether the recommendations translate into binding policy will depend on congressional priorities and the administration's willingness to add further friction to an already strained economic relationship with Beijing. For now, the proposals underscore how aerospace has emerged as a new front in the broader contest between the world's two largest economies.
